e-9492.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
e-9492.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/cd1ba2536264e122c84377a1892c3ca86dd8f273b2eab9ba0e2c53eeb504ef65.png)

  

Find a definite integral with respect to $\theta$ that's equivalent to $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-\sin{\theta}\,$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq  \pi,$ shown above.
e-9492.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

$$
L=	\int_C \,\textrm d s =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=1-\sin{\theta},$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = -\cos{\theta}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9493.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/a55339eae9b193813ab696538c85696ad5f4267e2e31513bdb2c8998cd711311.png)

  

Calculate $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2(1+\sin\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq {\pi},$ shown above.
e-9493.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

$$
L=	\int_C \,\textrm d s =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1+\sin\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\cos{\theta}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+4{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following identities:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})=1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting our integral using the above identities, we can evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =4\sqrt{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}((0+1)-(-1+0)) \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=4+cos⁡4θ for −π6≤θ≤7π6, shown above?

a
∫−π/67π/612+4cos⁡4θ+8sin2⁡4θdθ
b
∫−π/67π/612+6cos⁡4θ+10sin2⁡4θdθ
c
∫−π/67π/64+8cos⁡4θ+12sin2⁡4θdθ
d
∫−π/67π/610+6cos⁡4θ+12sin2⁡4θdθ
e
∫−π/67π/617+8cos⁡4θ+15sin2⁡4θdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: For polar arc length, ds = sqrt(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ. Here dr/dθ = -4 sin(4θ), so r²+(dr/dθ)² = (4+cos(4θ))²+16 sin²(4θ) = 17+8 cos(4θ)+15 sin²(4θ). Thus option e is correct.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/7dc83cbf45ec3025ad33552ce889c7ecb2daf73b426bc2fd10ec932f3311c92a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{7\pi }{6},$ shown above?
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{(4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +1+15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{17+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=4+cos⁡4θ for −π6≤θ≤7π6, shown above?

a
∫−π/67π/612+4cos⁡4θ+8sin2⁡4θdθ
b
∫−π/67π/612+6cos⁡4θ+10sin2⁡4θdθ
c
∫−π/67π/64+8cos⁡4θ+12sin2⁡4θdθ
d
∫−π/67π/610+6cos⁡4θ+12sin2⁡4θdθ
e
∫−π/67π/617+8cos⁡4θ+15sin2⁡4θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=4+cos⁡4θ, we have drdθ=−4sin⁡4θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/67π/6(4+cos⁡4θ)2+(−4sin⁡4θ)2dθ=∫−π/67π/616+8cos⁡4θ+cos2⁡4θ+16sin2⁡4θdθ=∫−π/67π/616+8cos⁡4θ+1+15sin2⁡4θdθ=∫−π/67π/617+8cos⁡4θ+15sin2⁡4θdθ.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/7dc83cbf45ec3025ad33552ce889c7ecb2daf73b426bc2fd10ec932f3311c92a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{7\pi }{6},$ shown above?
content.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{(4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +1+15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{17+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=sec3⁡θ for −π/2≤θ≤π/2 ?

a
∫0πsec2⁡θtan2⁡θdθ
b
∫−π/2π/2sec3⁡θ9+tan2⁡θdθ
c
∫0πsec3⁡θ1+tan2⁡θdθ
d
2∫0πsec3⁡θ1+sec2⁡θdθ
e
∫−π/2π/2sec3⁡θ1+9tan2⁡θdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Polar arc length uses ds = sqrt(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ. Since r = sec³(θ), dr/dθ = 3sec³(θ)tan(θ), giving ds = sec³(θ)sqrt(1+9tan²(θ)) dθ because sec(θ)>0 on the interval's interior. This is option e, interpreted as an improper integral at the endpoints; the arc length diverges to infinity.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\pi /2\le \theta \le \pi /2$ ?
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({sec}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta +9{sec}^{6}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=sec3⁡θ for −π/2≤θ≤π/2 ?

a
∫0πsec2⁡θtan2⁡θdθ
b
∫−π/2π/2sec3⁡θ9+tan2⁡θdθ
c
∫0πsec3⁡θ1+tan2⁡θdθ
d
2∫0πsec3⁡θ1+sec2⁡θdθ
e
∫−π/2π/2sec3⁡θ1+9tan2⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=sec3⁡θ we have
drdθ=3sec3⁡θtan⁡θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/2π/2(sec3⁡θ)2+(3sec3⁡θtan⁡θ)2dθ=∫−π/2−π/2sec6⁡θ+9sec6⁡θtan2⁡θdθ=∫−π/2π/2sec6⁡θ(1+9tan2⁡θ)dθ=∫−π/2π/2sec3⁡θ1+9tan2⁡θdθ.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\pi /2\le \theta \le \pi /2$ ?
content.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({sec}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta +9{sec}^{6}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: For polar arc length, ds = sqrt(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ. Here dr/dθ = 2sin(θ), so r²+(dr/dθ)² = (1−2cos(θ))²+4sin²(θ) = 5−4cos(θ). Integrating from π/3 to π gives option e.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/8fbf4c3074641b18d12dc7372378550f4c37e0b9b81843c2e57629c891a59263.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=1−2cos⁡θ for π3≤θ≤π, shown above?

a
∫π/3π1−2cos2⁡θdθ
b
∫π/3π5+4cos2⁡θdθ
c
∫π/3π1−2cos⁡θdθ
d
∫π/3π4−5cos2⁡θdθ
e
∫π/3π5−4cos⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1−2cos⁡θ, we have drdθ=2sin⁡θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/3π(1−2cos⁡θ)2+(2sin⁡θ)2dθ=∫π/3π1−4cos⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ+4sin2⁡θdθ=∫π/3π1−4cos⁡θ+4dθ=∫π/3π5−4cos⁡θdθ.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/8fbf4c3074641b18d12dc7372378550f4c37e0b9b81843c2e57629c891a59263.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?
content.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves

history.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1−2cos⁡θ, we have drdθ=2sin⁡θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/3π(1−2cos⁡θ)2+(2sin⁡θ)2dθ=∫π/3π1−4cos⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ+4sin2⁡θdθ=∫π/3π1−4cos⁡θ+4dθ=∫π/3π5−4cos⁡θdθ.

before.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=1+sin⁡4θ for 0≤θ≤2π ?

a
∫02π5+3sin⁡4θdθ
b
∫02π5−3cos⁡4θdθ
c
∫02π3+5sin⁡4θdθ
d
∫02π1−sin⁡4θdθ
e
∫02π5−3sin⁡4θdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Where r>0, r′=2cos(4θ)/sqrt(1+sin(4θ)). Thus r²+(r′)²=1+sin(4θ)+4(1−sin(4θ))=5−3sin(4θ), giving option e. Splitting the curve at its isolated zeros justifies the arc-length formula there. Options a and b also give the same integral by periodic shifts over the full interval; e directly expresses the derived arc-length element.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi $ ?
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta })^{2}+{(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )+\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta }{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1-{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )[1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta +4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=1+sin⁡4θ for 0≤θ≤2π ?

a
∫02π5+3sin⁡4θdθ
b
∫02π5−3cos⁡4θdθ
c
∫02π3+5sin⁡4θdθ
d
∫02π1−sin⁡4θdθ
e
∫02π5−3sin⁡4θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1+sin⁡4θ we have
drdθ=2cos⁡4θ1+sin⁡4θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫02π(1+sin⁡4θ)2+(2cos⁡4θ1+sin⁡4θ)2dθ=∫02π(1+sin⁡4θ)+4cos2⁡4θ1+sin⁡4θdθ=∫02π(1+sin⁡4θ)2+4(1−sin2⁡4θ)1+sin⁡4θdθ=∫02π(1+sin⁡4θ)2+4(1+sin⁡4θ)(1−sin⁡4θ)1+sin⁡4θdθ=∫02π(1+sin⁡4θ)[1+sin⁡4θ+4−4sin⁡4θ]1+sin⁡4θdθ=∫02π5−3sin⁡4θdθ.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms e: r′=2cos(4θ)/sqrt(1+sin(4θ)), so r²+(r′)²=1+sin(4θ)+4(1−sin(4θ))=5−3sin(4θ). Apply the arc-length formula piecewise at the isolated zeros of r. Options a and b have equal integral values by periodic shifts, but e directly gives the derived arc-length element.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi $ ?
content.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta })^{2}+{(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )+\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta }{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1-{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )[1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta +4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta })^{2}+{(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )+\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta }{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1-{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )[1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta +4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=2−4sin⁡θ for π2≤θ≤π, shown above?

a
2∫π/2π4−5cos⁡θdθ
b
2∫π/2π5−4sin⁡θdθ
c
2∫π/2π5+4cos⁡θdθ
d
2∫π/2π5−4cos⁡θdθ
e
∫π/2π5−4sin⁡θdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Since r′=−4cos(θ), r²+(r′)²=(2−4sin(θ))²+16cos²(θ)=4(5−4sin(θ)). Therefore ds=2sqrt(5−4sin(θ)) dθ, giving b. Option c has the same integral value under θ→3π/2−θ; b directly expresses the arc-length element.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/5b6490495c297b49d394b0f7c494fb35b710c8c4520ab898783877abdd079013.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +16}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{20-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=2−4sin⁡θ for π2≤θ≤π, shown above?

a
2∫π/2π4−5cos⁡θdθ
b
2∫π/2π5−4sin⁡θdθ
c
2∫π/2π5+4cos⁡θdθ
d
2∫π/2π5−4cos⁡θdθ
e
∫π/2π5−4sin⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=2−4sin⁡θ, we have drdθ=−4cos⁡θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/2π(2−4sin⁡θ)2+(−4cos⁡θ)2dθ=∫π/2π4−16sin⁡θ+16sin2⁡θ+16cos2⁡θdθ=∫π/2π4−16sin⁡θ+16dθ=∫π/2π20−16sin⁡θdθ=2∫π/2π5−4sin⁡θdθ.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/5b6490495c297b49d394b0f7c494fb35b710c8c4520ab898783877abdd079013.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?
content.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +16}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{20-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi .$
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta })^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\text{ }\,\pi \end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/624bb949d80c1da50cba951b00210a2a26aeb3c44d77d4c2eed69c8e3ba0f4d4.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4},$ shown above.
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =3(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

decision.explanation: With r=sec(θ), r′=sec(θ)tan(θ), so ds=sqrt(sec²(θ)(1+tan²(θ))) dθ=sec²(θ) dθ. Thus the arc length is [tan(θ)] from π/6 to π/3 = √3−√3/3 = 2√3/3, option e.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta (1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sec}^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta (1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sec}^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since r′=(1/4)e^{θ/4}, the arc-length element is sqrt(r²+(r′)²) dθ=(√17/4)e^{θ/4} dθ. Integrating from 0 to 2π gives √17(e^{π/2}−1), option c.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/b2ce73d5a44c834b5935596e85293eb92039b674746754317846488dbba8d930.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta /4}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ shown above.
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{\theta /4},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{\theta /4}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{({e}^{\theta /4})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{\theta /4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{e}^{\theta /2}+\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{\theta /2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{17}{16}\,{e}^{\theta /2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{e}^{\theta /4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{17}\,{e}^{\theta /4}\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{17}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{17}({e}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Calculate ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=eθ/4 for 0≤θ≤2π, shown above.

a
13(eπ/4−1)
b
5(eπ/4−1)
c
17(eπ/2−1)
d
10(eπ/2−1)
e
4(eπ/2−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=eθ/4, we have drdθ=14eθ/4.

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: ∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫02π(eθ/4)2+(14eθ/4)2dθ=∫02πeθ/2+116eθ/2dθ=∫02π1716eθ/2dθ=174∫02πeθ/4dθ=17eθ/4|02π=17(eπ/2−e0)=17(eπ/2−1).

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/b2ce73d5a44c834b5935596e85293eb92039b674746754317846488dbba8d930.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta /4}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ shown above.
content.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{\theta /4},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{\theta /4}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{({e}^{\theta /4})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{\theta /4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{e}^{\theta /2}+\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{\theta /2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{17}{16}\,{e}^{\theta /2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{e}^{\theta /4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{17}\,{e}^{\theta /4}\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{17}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{17}({e}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Calculate ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=θ2 for 0≤θ≤π, shown above.

a
(π2+4)3/2−42
b
(π+4)1/2−83
c
(π+2)1/2−86
d
(π+2)3/2−82
e
(π2+4)3/2−83
Submit

decision.explanation: For r=θ², r′=2θ, so ds=sqrt(θ⁴+4θ²) dθ=θsqrt(θ²+4) dθ since θ≥0. Therefore the arc length is [(θ²+4)^{3/2}/3]₀^π=((π²+4)^{3/2}−8)/3, option e.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/994b8cd2134d6d1e9a1e89559e462128c05fd5d3e7f4755c51931f3cf7f37268.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={\theta }^{2}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above.
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={\theta }^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{({\theta }^{2})}^{2}+{(2\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{4}+4{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}(4+{\theta }^{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\theta \sqrt{4+{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\theta \sqrt{4+{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\frac{{(4+{\theta }^{2})}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{({\pi }^{2}+4)}^{3/2}-8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=θ2, we have drdθ=2θ.

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: ∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π(θ2)2+(2θ)2dθ=∫0πθ4+4θ2dθ=∫0πθ2(4+θ2)dθ=∫0πθ4+θ2dθ=12∫0π2θ4+θ2dθ=(4+θ2)3/23|0π=(π2+4)3/2−83

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/994b8cd2134d6d1e9a1e89559e462128c05fd5d3e7f4755c51931f3cf7f37268.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={\theta }^{2}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above.
content.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={\theta }^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{({\theta }^{2})}^{2}+{(2\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{4}+4{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}(4+{\theta }^{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\theta \sqrt{4+{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\theta \sqrt{4+{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\frac{{(4+{\theta }^{2})}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{({\pi }^{2}+4)}^{3/2}-8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
